Q: mySQL Regexp with square brackets A:

I found one solution:

Create the pattern using CONCAT. One example searching '\ 0[6-9]:'

REGEXP CONCAT('\\ 0', '[', '6-9', ']:')

Q: Excel Index Match return most recent date A:

With OFFICE365 functions use the below formula:

=LET(rng,B4:E11,
prod,UNIQUE(TAKE(rng,,1)),
date,CHOOSECOLS(rng,2),
cost,BYROW(prod,LAMBDA(x,CHOOSECOLS(TAKE(SORT(FILTER(rng,CHOOSECOLS(rng,1)=x),2,-1),1),3))),
price,BYROW(prod,LAMBDA(x,CHOOSECOLS(TAKE(SORT(FILTER(rng,CHOOSECOLS(rng,1)=x),2,-1),1),4))),
maxdate,BYROW(prod,LAMBDA(x,MAX(FILTER(date,CHOOSECOLS(rng,1)=x)))),
HSTACK(prod,maxdate,cost,price))

One parameter is required the data range of the table to process.
prod returns the unique names of the products.
date selects the date column.
cost, price and maxdate are the arrays of the values belong to the max date by products.
The last line creates the table to return with all data.

Q: Capture stderr while passing stdout to a pipe A:

You have to exercise a little chicanery because a pipe puts your assignment in a subshell, which evaporates along with the value when the command is done. Breaking it out into steps -

echo Assigning
exec 3> >( grep -o 'May .*' )   # the downstream "pipe" filter on fd 3
foo=$( ls -l ./x bogus 2>&1 >&3 ) # the assignment, sending stdout to fd 3
exec 3>&-                       # close the fd if you don't need it anymore
echo Reporting
echo "[$foo]"                   # use the var

The output shows what grep spits out, the the echo.

Assigning
May 19 09:54 ./x
Reporting
[ls: cannot access 'bogus': No such file or directory]

Q: Optimizing imaging in WPF application A:

An example of preloading would be if the user views a folder or group of 100 images. But the window can only display 10 thumbnails at a time. Virtualization delays the loading of thumbnails until they are actually displayed. Preload would start creating thumbnails for images 10-19 if the user currently views 0-9, under the assumption that the user is likely to scroll to the next set of images. Or it might start creating thumbnails for the first 10 images in each folder/group under the assumption that the user is more likely to switch between folders than to start scrolling within a folder.

This is ofc a careful balance between using available resources to provide a better user experience, and wasting resources for loads that are never used. Something like a thread safe priority queue might be useful, so you can ensure requests for images you know the user wants to view are done before speculative requests. Or maybe a rate limit for the amount of preloads per second? Or limit of how many preloads can be queued at any time? Or maybe use thread priority?

Do note that "thousands of images" are not really that much. A 128x128 thumbnail might take ~1-10kb compressed. So keeping a thousand thumbnails in memory would only be 10Mb or so. How you cache thumbnails is another tradeoff to consider. Keeping decoded thumbnails in memory would be the fastest, but use most memory. Keeping compressed thumbnails in a database on the disk will use be slower and use less memory, but should still be much faster than loading, decoding and resampling the full sized image. Keeping compressed thumbnails in memory would be somewhere in between.

Q: Linux Command line: grep -e or -E? A:

I virtually never use -e, and you never have to that I can see. It's main use is for multiple patterns, which provides a simple syntax -
...| grep -e foo -e bar
But as already mentioned, you can grep 'foo\|bar or grep -E 'foo|bar'.
(I use -E a lot.)

One case where a lot of folk might appreciate it is when your argument starts with a dash.

$: printf -- '
--foo
bar
' | grep -e '-foo'
--foo

But you can get around that too. I prefer this:

$: printf -- '
--foo
bar
' | grep '[-]foo'
--foo

But what I prefer may not be what you prefer.

-e means "here's an expression"; -E means "use Extended pattern matching syntax."
